content: Garden angelica, scientifically known as Angelica archangelica (synonym: Archangelica officinalis var. Clarke), is a biennial plant belonging to the Apiaceae family, commonly referred to as the umbelliferous family. It is also known by alternative English names such as Holy Ghost, Wild Celery, and Norwegian Angelica. During its first year of growth, the plant produces only leaves. In its second year, it develops a fluted stem that can grow up to two meters (approximately six feet) in height. The leaves of garden angelica are composed of numerous small leaflets, which are divided into three primary groups. Each of these groups is further subdivided into three smaller groups. The edges of the leaflets are finely toothed or serrated. The plant produces small, numerous flowers that bloom in July. These flowers are yellowish or greenish in color and are arranged in large, globular umbels. The umbels bear pale yellow, oblong fruits. Garden angelica thrives in damp soil, preferably near rivers or water deposits. It should not be confused with the toxic Pastinaca sativa (commonly known as Wild Parsnip). The plant grows wild in northern regions of countries such as Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Greenland, the Faroe Islands, and Iceland. It is also cultivated in France, particularly in the Marais Poitevin, a marsh region near Niort in the Deux-Sèvres department. From the 10th century onward, garden angelica was cultivated as both a vegetable and a medicinal plant. It gained significant popularity in Scandinavia during the 12th century and remains in use today, particularly in Sami culture. The hollow stems of the plant can be fashioned into a flute-like instrument with a clarinet-like sound, likely as a toy for children. The renowned botanist Linnaeus noted that the Sami people used garden angelica in reindeer milk. Other uses include its application as a spice. In 1602, garden angelica was introduced to Niort, a region that had recently suffered from the plague, and it has remained popular there ever since. The plant is used in the production of liqueurs such as Chartreuse, Bénédictine, Vermouth, and Dubonnet. It is also incorporated into dishes like omelets and trout, as well as in jams. The long, bright green stems of the plant are often candied and used as decorations. In Persian cuisine, the petals of garden angelica are included in the spice mixture Advieh to flavor rice dishes, as well as chicken and bean dishes. Garden angelica is unique among the Umbelliferae family due to its pervasive aromatic odor, which is described as a pleasant perfume distinct from fennel, parsley, anise, caraway, or chervil. Some historical writers have compared its scent to musk, while others liken it to juniper. Even the roots of the plant are fragrant and are considered one of the principal aromatic plants of European origin. While all parts of the plant share the same flavor, the active principles in the roots are thought to be more stable than those in other parts of the plant. The plant contains a variety of chemical compounds with demonstrated medicinal properties. Chewing on garden angelica or drinking tea brewed from it induces local anesthesia and enhances the immune system. It has been shown to be effective against various bacterial, fungal, and even viral infections. The essential oil extracted from the roots of Angelica archangelica contains β-terebangelene (C10H16) and other terpenes. The oil from the seeds also contains β-terebangelene, along with methylethylacetic acid and hydroxymyristic acid. Both the seeds and roots of garden angelica are sometimes used in the production of absinthe. The name archangelica is derived from the Greek word arkhangelos, meaning archangel, based on the myth that the Archangel Gabriel revealed the plant's medicinal uses. In Finnish, the plant is called väinönputki, in Sami it is known as fádnu, boska, or rássi, and in English, it is referred to as garden angelica. In German, it is called arznei-engelwurz, in Dutch grote engelwortel, in Farsi gol-par, in Swedish kvanne, in Norwegian kvann, in Danish kvann, and in Icelandic hvönn.
